claim: A large fraction of genomes is transcribed according to deep sequencing analyses.
source: Deep sequencing analyses have shown that a large fraction of genomes is transcribed, but the significance of this transcription is much debated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature on deep sequencing analyses.

claim: At a given sequencing depth, transcriptome coverage becomes saturated within a taxon.
source: Using deep RNA sequencing we find that at a given sequencing depth transcriptome coverage becomes saturated within a taxon, but keeps extending when compared between taxa, even at this very shallow phylogenetic level.
evidence: This claim is based on the RNA sequencing data presented in the study.

claim: Transcriptome coverage keeps extending when compared between taxa at shallow phylogenetic levels.
source: Using deep RNA sequencing we find that at a given sequencing depth transcriptome coverage becomes saturated within a taxon, but keeps extending when compared between taxa, even at this very shallow phylogenetic level.
evidence: This claim is based on the RNA sequencing data comparing multiple taxa.

claim: There is high turnover of transcriptional states between taxa.
source: Our data show a high turnover of transcriptional states between taxa and that no major transcript-free islands exist across evolutionary time.
evidence: This claim is based on the comparative transcriptome data across taxa.

claim: No major transcript-free islands exist across evolutionary time.
source: Our data show a high turnover of transcriptional states between taxa and that no major transcript-free islands exist across evolutionary time.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of transcriptome coverage across evolutionary time.

claim: The entire genome can be transcribed into poly-adenylated RNA when viewed at an evolutionary time scale.
source: This suggests that the entire genome can be transcribed into poly-adenylated RNA when viewed at an evolutionary time scale.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing high turnover and lack of transcript-free islands.

claim: Any part of the non-coding genome can potentially become subject to evolutionary functionalization via de novo gene evolution within relatively short evolutionary time spans.
source: We conclude that any part of the non-coding genome can potentially become subject to evolutionary functionalization via de novo gene evolution within relatively short evolutionary time spans.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing pervasive transcription and turnover.

claim: Much larger portions of the genome are transcribed than would have been predicted from annotated exons.
source: Genome-wide surveys have provided evidence for 'pervasive transcription', i.e., much larger portions of the genome are transcribed than would have been predicted from annotated exons (Clark et al., 2011; Hangauer et al., 2013; Kellis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genome-wide surveys.

claim: Most additional transcripts are expected to be non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs).
source: Most are expected to be non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) of which some have been shown to be functional.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about pervasive transcription.

claim: Some lncRNAs have been shown to be functional.
source: Most are expected to be non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) of which some have been shown to be functional.
evidence: This claim is based on existing literature on lncRNA function.

claim: The general conservation level of additional transcripts tends to be low.
source: However, the general conservation level of these additional transcripts tends to be low, which raises the question of their evolutionary turnover dynamics (Kutter et al., 2012; Kapusta and Feschotte, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on transcript conservation.

claim: Additional transcripts could be a source for de novo gene formation via a proto-gene stage.
source: They are currently receiving additional attention, since they could be a source for de novo gene formation via a proto-gene stage (Carvunis et al., 2012; Ruiz-Orera et al., 2014; Neme and Tautz, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on de novo gene formation.

claim: De novo gene emergence shows particularly high rates in the youngest lineages.
source: It has been shown that de novo gene emergence shows particularly high rates in the youngest lineages (Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011), indicating that there is high turnover of such transcripts and genes between closely related species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on de novo gene emergence rates.

claim: There is high turnover of transcripts and genes between closely related species.
source: It has been shown that de novo gene emergence shows particularly high rates in the youngest lineages (Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011), indicating that there is high turnover of such transcripts and genes between closely related species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high rates of de novo gene emergence in young lineages.

claim: Comparative studies of de novo genes between Drosophila species have confirmed high turnover.
source: Indeed, comparative studies of de novo genes between Drosophila species (Palmieri et al., 2014) and within Drosophila populations (Zhao et al., 2014) have confirmed this.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative studies in Drosophila.

claim: Single mutational events can generate new transcripts in previously non-coding regions.
source: A number of possibilities have been discussed by which new transcripts are generated in previously non-coding regions, including single mutational events, stabilization of bi-directional transcription and insertion of transposable elements with promotor activity (Brosius, 2005; Gotea et al., 2013; Neme and Tautz, 2013; Wu and Sharp, 2013; Sundaram et al., 2014; Ruiz-Orera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mechanisms of transcript generation.

claim: Single step mutations can be sufficient to generate a stable transcript in a region that was previously not transcribed and translated.
source: Detailed analyses of specific cases of emergence of a de novo gene have shown that single step mutations can be sufficient to generate a stable transcript in a region that was previously not transcribed and translated (Heinen et al., 2009; Knowles and McLysaght, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to detailed case studies.

claim: The unequivocal identification of de novo transcript emergence can only be made in a comparison between very closely related evolutionary lineages.
source: The unequivocal identification of de novo transcript emergence can only be made in a comparison between very closely related evolutionary lineages, where orthologous genomic regions can be fully aligned, even for the neutrally evolving parts of the genome (Tautz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a methodological principle.

claim: Available genome and transcriptome data for mammals and insects are too far apart to allow a comprehensive genome-wide assessment of de novo transcript emergence.
source: While the available genome and transcriptome data for mammals and insects are sufficient to screen for specific cases of de novo transcript emergence, they are still too far apart of each other to allow a comprehensive genome-wide assessment.
evidence: This claim is based on assessment of existing data and justifies the current study.

claim: The study samples span 10 million years of divergence.
source: Altogether they span 10 million years of divergence, which corresponds to an average of 6% nucleotide difference for the most distant comparisons.
evidence: This claim is based on the phylogenetic sampling design of the study.

claim: The most distant comparisons correspond to an average of 6% nucleotide difference.
source: Altogether they span 10 million years of divergence, which corresponds to an average of 6% nucleotide difference for the most distant comparisons.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence divergence data.

claim: The common genome represents 71.7% of the total reference genome length.
source: It represents 71.7% of the total reference genome length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on genome mapping data shown in the figure.

claim: About a third of the total genome length is not analyzed, corresponding to highly repetitive parts.
source: Hence, we are nominally not analyzing about a third of the total genome length, but this corresponds to the highly repetitive parts for which unique and reliable mapping of transcriptomic reads would not be possible.
evidence: This claim is based on the methodological approach and genome composition.

claim: Testis and brain harbor the largest diversity of transcripts.
source: Previous studies had shown that testis and brain harbor the largest diversity of transcripts (Necsulea and Kaessmann, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The study sequenced only the poly-A+ fraction of the RNA.
source: We sequenced only the poly-A+ fraction of the RNA, i.e., our focus is on coding and non-coding exons in processed RNA.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the study design.

claim: Liver has the lowest overall read coverage among the three tissues analyzed.
source: Among the three tissues analyzed, liver has the lowest overall read coverage while brain and testis have similar overall levels (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is based on the sequencing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Brain and testis have similar overall levels of read coverage.
source: Among the three tissues analyzed, liver has the lowest overall read coverage while brain and testis have similar overall levels (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is based on the sequencing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Combining data from all three tissues increases overall coverage similarly to triplicating read depth for one tissue.
source: Combining the data from all three tissues or triplicating the read depth for one tissue (brain) increases the overall coverage in a similar way (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of sequencing strategies shown in Figure 2.

claim: The total coverage across all tissues and sequencing runs amounts to an average of 50.0 ± 2.5% per taxon.
source: Figure 2F shows the total coverage across all tissues and all sequencing runs, which amounts to an average of 50.0 ± 2.5% per taxon.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined sequencing data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A very similar coverage is observed in all taxa for each tissue and in the combined set.
source: Hence, for each tissue, as well as in this combined set, we observe a very similar coverage in all taxa, with only a slight increase in the low expressed fraction for the most distant comparisons (see also legend Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the coverage data across taxa.

claim: Between 1 and 7% of transcribed windows are unique to one taxon only.
source: Between 1 and 7% of transcribed windows are unique to one taxon only, with the more distant taxa showing the higher percentages (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of taxon-specific transcripts shown in Figure 3.

claim: More distant taxa show higher percentages of taxon-specific transcripts.
source: Between 1 and 7% of transcribed windows are unique to one taxon only, with the more distant taxa showing the higher percentages (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of taxon-specific transcripts shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most taxon-specific transcripts are lowly expressed (<10 reads per window).
source: Most of these taxon-specific transcripts are lowly expressed (<10 reads per window), but the more distant taxa (MAT and APO in Figure 3I,J) show also some more highly expressed ones.
evidence: This claim is based on the expression level analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A total of 6566 windows with read counts >50 occur in a single taxon only.
source: We find a total of 6566 windows with read counts >50 that occur in a single taxon only, mostly in the long branches leading to MAT (1638 windows) and APO (4485 windows), but some also between the most closely related taxa (43 windows for DOM, including populations; 38 windows for MUS, including populations).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of highly expressed taxon-specific transcripts.

claim: Approximately 18% of windows show transcripts shared across all taxa.
source: Approximately 18% of windows show transcripts shared across all taxa.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of conserved transcripts.

claim: Shared transcripts across all taxa include most of the very highly expressed ones (>100 reads per window).
source: These include most of the very highly expressed ones (>100 reads per window), but also a fraction of the low expressed ones (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the expression level analysis of conserved transcripts shown in Figure 3.

claim: Shared transcripts are enriched in annotated genes, especially in exons of protein coding genes.
source: They are also enriched in annotated genes, especially in exons of protein coding genes, but also in non-coding genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on annotation enrichment analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Windows sharing between 2 and 9 taxa constitute cumulatively the largest fraction (between 26 and 33% of whole genome coverage).
source: This class constitutes cumulatively the largest fraction (between 26 and 33% of whole genome coverage - Figure 3), supporting the notion of a fast turnover of most of the transcribed regions between taxa.
evidence: This claim is based on the quantitative analysis of transcript sharing shown in Figure 3.

claim: The taxon-specific turnover of transcripts is reflected in a distance tree of shared coverage.
source: The taxon-specific turnover of transcripts is also reflected in a distance tree of shared coverage.
evidence: This claim is based on the phylogenetic analysis of transcript sharing.

claim: Taxa that are phylogenetically closer to each other share more transcripts.
source: Taxa that are phylogenetically closer to each other share more transcripts, i.e. the tree topology mimics that of a phylogenetic tree based on molecular sequence divergence (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of transcript-based and molecular phylogenies shown in Figure 4.

claim: The turnover of transcripts is not random, but time dependent.
source: This implies that the turnover of the transcripts is not random, but time dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phylogenetic pattern of transcript sharing.

claim: The relative branch lengths are much extended for the more closely related taxa compared to the molecular distances.
source: However, the relative branch lengths are much extended for the more closely related taxa compared to the molecular distances, implying that there is a particularly high turnover between them.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of branch lengths in different phylogenies.

claim: There is a particularly high turnover of transcripts between closely related taxa.
source: However, the relative branch lengths are much extended for the more closely related taxa compared to the molecular distances, implying that there is a particularly high turnover between them.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the extended branch lengths in the transcript-based tree.

claim: Singletons constitute about 2–12% of the common windows when assessed on a per sample basis.
source: Depending on read depth and tissue, they constitute about 2–12% of the common windows when assessed on a per sample basis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the singleton analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Most singletons in a given sample were re-detected in another tissue or another taxon.
source: However, most of these singletons in a given sample were re-detected in another tissue or another taxon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), such that less than 2% are present in a given taxon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and less than 7% cumulatively throughout the whole dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the re-detection analysis of singletons shown in the figure supplements.

claim: 88% of singleton-based branch length is influenced by sampling variance.
source: We find that 88% of the branch length is influenced by sampling variance, while the remaining 12% still recover the expected topology (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on the variance analysis of singleton reads shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At the 100 Mill read level, there is a noticeable effect of sampling variance, but this does not erase the underlying signal.
source: Hence, at the 100 Mill read level, we have a noticeable effect of sampling variance, but this does not erase the underlying signal.
evidence: This claim is based on the sampling variance analysis.

claim: The addition of taxa leads to a further increase in transcriptomic coverage.
source: The addition of taxa indeed leads to a further increase in transcriptomic coverage, with a generalized linear model best describing the data as increasing in a logarithmic fashion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on the rarefaction analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transcriptomic coverage increases in a logarithmic fashion with addition of taxa.
source: The addition of taxa indeed leads to a further increase in transcriptomic coverage, with a generalized linear model best describing the data as increasing in a logarithmic fashion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical modeling of the rarefaction data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: An asymptotic behavior is observed for increasing depth of sequencing.
source: In contrast, we observe an asymptotic behavior of the curve for increasing depth of sequencing, with apparent saturation reached at 84.1%, close to the 83.2% that we have already achieved (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on the sequencing depth analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sequencing depth saturation is reached at 84.1%.
source: In contrast, we observe an asymptotic behavior of the curve for increasing depth of sequencing, with apparent saturation reached at 84.1%, close to the 83.2% that we have already achieved (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on the saturation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Random transcriptional noise or deficiencies in sampling low level transcripts are not major factors in the analysis.
source: First, random transcriptional noise (technical or biological) or deficiencies in sampling low level transcripts should not be major factors in our analysis, since saturation with sequencing depth would not be possible under a singleton dominated regime.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the saturation analysis.

claim: Low level transcripts (including singletons) have detectable biological signal.
source: Furthermore, low level transcripts (including singletons) have detectable biological signal (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on the singleton analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The data are consistent with evolutionary turnover leading to steady and almost unlimited transcriptional exploration of the genome.
source: Second, the data are consistent with the above outlined ideas that the evolutionary turnover leads to steady – and almost unlimited – transcriptional exploration of the genome, when summed over multiple parallel evolutionary lineages and taxa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rarefaction and saturation analyses.

claim: The maximum observed length of non-transcribed regions is 6 kb.
source: We find that the maximum observed length of non-transcribed regions is 6 kb (Figure 6), suggesting that apparent transcriptional deserts in one taxon are readily accessible to transcription in other taxa, at least for the non-repetitive windows of the genome that are analyzed here.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of non-transcribed regions shown in Figure 6.

claim: Apparent transcriptional deserts in one taxon are readily accessible to transcription in other taxa.
source: We find that the maximum observed length of non-transcribed regions is 6 kb (Figure 6), suggesting that apparent transcriptional deserts in one taxon are readily accessible to transcription in other taxa, at least for the non-repetitive windows of the genome that are analyzed here.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the small maximum size of non-transcribed regions.

claim: Many additional transcripts have sufficient stability to reflect a phylogenetic distance distribution that mimics the phylogeny of the taxa.
source: Here we were able to trace the turnover of these extra transcripts. Our data suggest that many have sufficient stability to reflect a phylogenetic distance distribution that mimics the phylogeny of the taxa.
evidence: This claim is based on the phylogenetic analysis of transcript sharing.

claim: Additional transcripts should not simply be considered as noise.
source: Hence, they should not simply be considered as noise.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phylogenetic signal in transcript turnover.

claim: The lifetime of additional transcripts should be sufficient to expose them to evolutionary testing.
source: Rather, their lifetime should be sufficient to expose them to evolutionary testing and in this way they become a substrate for de novo evolution of genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stability and phylogenetic signal of transcripts.

claim: Additional transcripts become a substrate for de novo evolution of genes.
source: Rather, their lifetime should be sufficient to expose them to evolutionary testing and in this way they become a substrate for de novo evolution of genes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the properties of the transcripts.

claim: Transcripts have high turnover between taxa if they do not acquire a function.
source: On the other hand, they appear to have only a limited lifetime in case they do not acquire a function, i.e. there is also high turnover of the transcribed regions between taxa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed turnover patterns.

claim: Within a timespan of a few million years practically the whole genome is covered by transcription at some point in time.
source: This turnover has as a consequence that within a timespan of a few million years practically the whole genome is covered by transcription at some point in time, i.e. no major transcript-free islands exist.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the turnover and rarefaction analyses.

claim: If more tissues and life stages were sampled, one would expect an even higher coverage of the genome within a given taxon.
source: If more tissues and more life stages were sampled, one would expect an even higher coverage of the genome within a given taxon.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the current sampling.

claim: The turnover of transcribed regions between taxa would also apply to other tissues and stages.
source: Still, we expect that the turnover of transcribed regions between taxa would also apply to the other tissues and stages, i.e. evolutionary testing of new transcripts would relate to all tissues and stages.
evidence: This is a speculative claim extrapolating from the current findings.

claim: ENCODE projects have confirmed pervasive transcription at the single-taxon level.
source: Such deep analyses have been done in the ENCODE projects (http://www.genome.gov/10005107) and they have confirmed pervasive transcription (Clark et al., 2011; Hangauer et al., 2013; Kellis et al., 2014) at the single-taxon level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ENCODE project publications.

claim: The set of conserved genes across taxa may maintain expression levels across larger evolutionary distances.
source: This turnover is contrasted by the set of conserved genes across taxa, for which even the expression levels may be maintained across larger evolutionary distances (Pervouchine et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on conserved gene expression.

claim: There is a particularly large number of lineage-specific transcripts among the most closely related taxa.
source: We see a particularly large number of lineage-specific transcripts among the most closely related taxa.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of taxon-specific transcripts.

claim: At very short evolutionary distances (thousands of years) there is an even higher turnover of transcripts than at longer time frames (millions of years).
source: Although this is partially influenced by sampling variance of low expressed transcripts (Figure 4C), this suggests that at the very short evolutionary distances (thousands of years) there is an even higher turnover of transcripts than at the longer time frames (millions of years).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the branch length patterns in phylogenetic trees.

claim: Weak selection could act against many newly arising transcripts.
source: Such a pattern of unequal rates suggests that weak selection could act against many newly arising transcripts, such that they can exist for a short time at a population scale, but not over an extended time.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed turnover patterns.

claim: The presence of new transcripts will be polymorphic at the population level.
source: Hence, we expect that the presence of such transcripts will be polymorphic at the population level, similar as it has been shown in Drosophila (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by analogy to Drosophila studies.

claim: A fraction of new transcripts interacts with other genes and cellular processes.
source: We expect that a fraction of new transcripts interacts with other genes and cellular processes, either via providing a positive function or via being slightly deleterious.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about transcript function.

claim: Many RNAs initially classified as non-coding can be associated to ribosomes and are likely translated.
source: The analysis of ribosome profiling data has shown that many RNAs that were initially classified as non-coding can be associated to ribosomes, i.e. are likely translated (Wilson and Masel, 2011; Carvunis et al., 2012; Ruiz-Orera et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ribosome profiling studies.

claim: De novo genes frequently act first as RNA and acquire open reading frames only at a later stage.
source: On the other hand, when tracing the origin of de novo genes, one finds frequently that they act first as RNA and acquire open reading frames only at a later stage (Cai et al., 2008; Kapranov and St. Laurent, 2012; Reinhardt et al., 2013 - see discussion in Schlötterer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on de novo gene evolution.

claim: Some de novo evolved genes in Drosophila have assumed essential functions such that knockouts are lethal.
source: For some of the de novo evolved genes in Drosophila it has been shown that they have assumed essential functions for the organism, such that knockouts of them are lethal (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a Drosophila study.

claim: The de novo evolution process has been active throughout evolutionary history.
source: Global analyses of new gene emergence trends suggest that the de novo evolution process has been active throughout the evolutionary history (Neme and Tautz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a global analysis study.

claim: The possibility of a transition from new transcript emergence over acquisition of reading frames towards assuming essential genetic functions is well documented.
source: Hence, the possibility of a transition from new transcript emergence over acquisition of reading frames towards assuming essential genetic functions is well documented.
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of cited literature.

claim: The idea that many de novo transcripts are slightly deleterious is concordant with cellular processes maintaining a balance between RNA transcription and degradation.
source: The idea that many de novo transcripts are slightly deleterious is concordant with the fact that various cellular processes maintain a balance between RNA transcription and degradation (Houseley and Tollervey, 2009; Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on RNA homeostasis.

claim: Several molecular pathways exist that degrade excess transcripts in yeast and mammals.
source: In yeast and mammals it has been shown that several molecular pathways exist that degrade excess transcripts, in particular the ones from bidirectional promoter activity (Jensen et al., 2013; Wu and Sharp, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on transcript degradation.

claim: Low levels of transcripts found by deep sequencing could alternatively be due to fast targeting by a degradation machinery rather than low transcription.
source: Hence, the fact that many of the transcripts found by deep sequencing occur only at low levels does not necessarily imply a low level of transcription, but could alternatively be due to fast targeting by a degradation machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the interpretation of low-level transcripts.

claim: Emergence, functionalization and decay of gene functions should be seen as an evolutionary life cycle of genes.
source: Our results provide an evolutionary dynamics perspective where emergence, functionalization and decay of gene functions should be seen as an evolutionary life cycle of genes (Neme and Tautz, 2014).
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the study results and cited work.

claim: De novo gene birth should be considered as an inherent property of the transcriptional apparatus.
source: De novo gene birth should no longer be considered as the result of unlikely circumstances, but rather as an inherent property of the transcriptional apparatus and thus a mechanism for testing and revealing hidden adaptive potential in genomes (Brosius, 2005; Masel and Siegal, 2009).
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the study results and cited work.

claim: Any non-genic part of the genome has the possibility to become useful at some time.
source: Within this evolutionary perspective, any non-genic part of the genome has the possibility to become useful at some time.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the study's findings.

claim: The two European populations of Mus musculus domesticus diverged about 3,000 years ago.
source: The youngest divergence point sampled, at about 3,000 years, corresponds to the split between two European populations of Mus musculus domesticus(Cucchi et al., 2005) one from France (Massif Central = DOMMC) and one from Germany (Cologne-Bonn area = DOMCB) (Ihle et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mouse population history.

claim: European M. m. domesticus populations diverged from an ancestral population in Iran about 12,000 years ago.
source: These European populations in turn have diverged from an ancestral M. m. domesticus population in Iran (Ahvaz = DOMAH) about 12,000 years ago (Hardouin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on mouse population history.

claim: M. m. domesticus has diverged from M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus about 0.4 to 0.5 million years ago.
source: M. m. domesticus has diverged from M. m. musculus and Mus musculus castaneus about 0.4 to 0.5 million years ago, with a subsequent divergence, not long after, between M. m. musculus and M. m. castaneus (Suzuki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: Mus spicilegus has an estimated divergence of 1.2 million years.
source: To account for longer divergence times, we included Mus spicilegus (SPI; estimated divergence of 1.2 million years); Mus spretus (SPR; estimated divergence of 1.7 million years)(Suzuki et al., 2013); Mus matteyii (MAT; subgenus Nannomys), the North African miniature mouse (estimated divergence of 6.6 million years) (Catzeflis and Denys, 1992; Lecompte et al., 2008), and Apodemus uralensis, the Ural field mouse (APO; estimated divergence of 10.6 million years) (Lecompte et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Mus spretus has an estimated divergence of 1.7 million years.
source: To account for longer divergence times, we included Mus spicilegus (SPI; estimated divergence of 1.2 million years); Mus spretus (SPR; estimated divergence of 1.7 million years)(Suzuki et al., 2013); Mus matteyii (MAT; subgenus Nannomys), the North African miniature mouse (estimated divergence of 6.6 million years) (Catzeflis and Denys, 1992; Lecompte et al., 2008), and Apodemus uralensis, the Ural field mouse (APO; estimated divergence of 10.6 million years) (Lecompte et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Mus mattheyi has an estimated divergence of 6.6 million years.
source: To account for longer divergence times, we included Mus spicilegus (SPI; estimated divergence of 1.2 million years); Mus spretus (SPR; estimated divergence of 1.7 million years)(Suzuki et al., 2013); Mus matteyii (MAT; subgenus Nannomys), the North African miniature mouse (estimated divergence of 6.6 million years) (Catzeflis and Denys, 1992; Lecompte et al., 2008), and Apodemus uralensis, the Ural field mouse (APO; estimated divergence of 10.6 million years) (Lecompte et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Apodemus uralensis has an estimated divergence of 10.6 million years.
source: To account for longer divergence times, we included Mus spicilegus (SPI; estimated divergence of 1.2 million years); Mus spretus (SPR; estimated divergence of 1.7 million years)(Suzuki et al., 2013); Mus matteyii (MAT; subgenus Nannomys), the North African miniature mouse (estimated divergence of 6.6 million years) (Catzeflis and Denys, 1992; Lecompte et al., 2008), and Apodemus uralensis, the Ural field mouse (APO; estimated divergence of 10.6 million years) (Lecompte et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to phylogenetic studies.

claim: NextGenMap performs extremely well with divergences of over 10% compared to other standard mapping software.
source: Transcriptome and genome sequencing reads were aligned against the mm10 version of the mouse reference genome (Waterston et al., 2002) from UCSC (Karolchik et al., 2014) using NextGenMap which performs extremely well with divergences of over 10% compared to other standard mapping software (Sedlazeck et al., 2013), as confirmed by our own simulations (Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and validation simulations.
